title: Consequences Alone Won't Change Challenging Behavior
author: Debbie Leonard
summary: Debbie Leonard draws on teaching in a boys' reformatory and in a violent urban middle school basement to argue that standard classroom-management advice fails when teachers and students are both emotionally flooded. Be consistent and stay calm is sound, she says, but it goes out the window by the fifth repetition, and students who have responded one way for years will not change on command. Habit research suggests a new habit takes two to five months, so repeated negative consequences cannot do the job alone. Her remedy is to teach, model, and practice alternatives the way athletes and musicians rehearse, starting each class with three to five minutes of breathing-based calm. She also urges pausing a lesson to discuss a real conflict, what happened, what emotions were involved, and what else could have been done. The piece frames this as time saved rather than time lost, since every disruption stops learning for everyone.
points: Expert advice such as being consistent and staying calm is correct but collapses under frustration, so teachers need a practised alternative rather than a reminder.
Consequences may stop a behavior briefly, yet they never teach students what to do instead, so the same behavior returns.
A daily three to five minute focus and relaxation routine calms students and the teacher alike, and gives students a skill they keep for life.
Students need rehearsal of alternative responses in the way athletes and musicians practise, because new habits take months to form.
Real classroom conflicts are the curriculum for this practice, so pausing for a five minute class discussion costs less than repeated redirection.
quotes: Typical expert advice for classroom management is familiar: Be consistent. Set clear expectations. Don’t engage in power struggles. Stay calm.
And the same is true for our students. We can’t expect a student who’s been responding one way for years to suddenly do something different because we’ve told them to.
Not a day, not a week, and certainly not because we’ve repeated the same negative consequence for the hundredth time.
We’d start every class with three to five minutes of focus and relaxation. Teach students to use their breathing to calm their minds and bodies and prepare for learning.
Telling them to stop arguing, sending them to the office, writing them up... those consequences may stop the behavior temporarily, but they don’t teach students what to do differently the next time.
Why would we expect students to change their behavior without the same opportunities?
When a disruption occurs, learning stops for everyone, not just the students involved.
